topic: The Knowledge Vault: How MLPs in Transformers Store Facts
target_audience: University students in Computer Science or Data Science with basic linear algebra knowledge

outline.topic: The Knowledge Vault: How MLPs in Transformers Store Facts
outline.target_audience: University students in Computer Science or Data Science with basic linear algebra knowledge

sections.title: The Mystery of Model Memory
sections.content: Introduce the concept that while Attention mechanisms handle relationships between words, the Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) layers act as the 'long-term memory' or 'knowledge store' of the Transformer. Frame the central question: Where does the model keep the fact that 'The capital of France is Paris'?
sections.example: Imagine a librarian (the Transformer) walking through a giant library. The Attention mechanism is the librarian's eyes looking at the current book, but the MLP is the rows of bookshelves containing the actual data.

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Residual Stream Conveyor Belt
sections.content: Explain the 'Residual Stream' as a continuous flow of information (a vector) that passes through each layer. The MLP doesn't replace this information; it 'reads' from it and 'writes' updates to it via addition.
sections.example: A conveyor belt carries a white box labeled 'Subject: France'. As it passes the MLP station, a robot arm adds a sticker saying 'Capital: Paris' to the side of the box.

sections.title: The First Layer: Pattern Matching (The Keys)
sections.content: Introduce the first linear transformation (W1). Mathematically, this is a set of 'Key' vectors. When the input vector (the query) aligns with a Key vector through a dot product, it 'activates'. Use a graphical representation of vectors pointing in similar directions to show 'matching'.
sections.example: If the input vector represents 'The capital of...', it triggers a specific neuron in W1 that specifically recognizes 'Geopolitical Capitals'.

sections.title: The Activation Gate: Filtering Knowledge
sections.content: Discuss the non-linear activation function (like GELU or ReLU). Explain that this acts as a threshold: if the 'Key' matches well enough, the gate opens; if not, the information is suppressed. This prevents irrelevant 'facts' from being added to the stream.
sections.example: Think of a security guard who only allows people with a 'Paris-shaped' key to pass through the gate to the next room.

sections.title: The Second Layer: Retrieving the Fact (The Values)
sections.content: Introduce the second linear transformation (W2). Each neuron in the first layer is associated with a 'Value' vector in the second layer. If a Key is activated, its corresponding Value (the actual factual data) is projected back into the residual stream.
sections.example: Once the 'Capital Pattern' key is matched, the model pulls the specific 'Paris' vector out of its 'Value' drawer and adds it to the information package on the conveyor belt.

sections.title: Summary: The Key-Value Memory Store
sections.content: Synthesize the process: Input -> Match Key (W1) -> Gate (Activation) -> Retrieve Value (W2). Explain that a Transformer has millions of these tiny 'Key-Value' pairs distributed across layers, forming a massive, programmable associative memory.
sections.example: A visual flow-chart: 'Input: Eiffel Tower' -> 'W1: Recognizes Landmark' -> 'GELU: High Confidence' -> 'W2: Adds [Location: Paris]' -> 'Output: Paris'.

storyboard.title: The Mystery of Model Memory
lecture_lines: Attention connects words, but where are facts stored?
Transformers use MLP layers as a vast knowledge vault.
How does the model remember that Paris is in France?
animations: Fade in title "The Mystery of Model Memory" in light blue #ADD8E6.
Display a central book icon labeled "Context" representing Attention's focus.
Show a vast background grid labeled "MLP: The Knowledge Store".

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: The Residual Stream Conveyor Belt
lecture_lines: Information flows through layers via the residual stream.
MLP layers read from this stream to process data.
They write updates by adding new vectors back in.
animations: Draw a white horizontal line labeled "Residual Stream" at bottom.
Slide a white box labeled "Vector" along the line.
Show an arrow from the vector up to "MLP Block".

storyboard.title: The First Layer: Pattern Matching (The Keys)
lecture_lines: The first MLP layer uses a matrix of keys.
Input vectors act as queries searching for a match.
We calculate the dot product between queries and keys.
High alignment triggers a specific neuron in the layer.
This detects patterns like "The capital city of."
animations: Show a central yellow vector #FFFF00 labeled "Query (Input)".
Surround it with green vectors #00FF00 labeled "Key Vectors (W1)".
Animate the yellow Query vector rotating to align with one Key.
Highlight the matching Key with a white glow #FFFFFF.
Display the dot product symbol between Query and Key.

storyboard.title: The Activation Gate: Filtering Knowledge
lecture_lines: The GELU function acts as a nonlinear activation gate.
Only strong matches pass through to the next stage.
This filter suppresses noise and irrelevant factual data.
animations: Draw a red horizontal line #FF0000 labeled "Activation Threshold".
Move a bright signal pulse from below toward the line.
The line turns green #00FF00 as the pulse passes through.

storyboard.title: The Second Layer: Retrieving the Fact (The Values)
lecture_lines: The second layer contains a corresponding bank of values.
Each activated key neuron links to a value vector.
If a key matches, its value is retrieved.
This value vector represents the factual answer like "Paris."
The retrieved fact is added back to the stream.
animations: Display a grid of blue vectors #00BFFF labeled "Value Vectors (W2)".
Highlight the specific Value vector linked to the active Key.
Animate this Value vector (labeled "Paris") moving downward.
Show a plus sign as Value joins the Residual Stream.
Update the Residual Stream box label to "Vector + Information".

storyboard.title: Summary: The Key-Value Memory Store
lecture_lines: MLPs operate as a programmable associative memory system.
Key vectors detect patterns while value vectors store facts.
The activation gate controls the flow between them.
Millions of these pairs form the model's global memory.
Together, they transform input queries into factual knowledge.
animations: Show three connected blocks: W1 Match, GELU Gate, W2 Retrieve.
Animate a pulse traveling through the blocks from left to right.
Display final text "A Massive Key-Value Memory Store" in #FFFFFF.
